Supervisor's note, Thursday. Sudha, customer support floor.
Two complaints reached me this week, and I nearly handled them the wrong way round.
Ritesh came in calm, as he does most weeks. His story: the night team dumps tickets on him, nobody values him, he is always left out. It is the fifth such story since January. Each has a different villain and the same sufferer.
Pankaj came in red-faced, almost shouting that his overtime hours had been logged under someone else's name. I nearly told him to come back when he could speak calmly.
I checked the logs before responding. Pankaj was right: his hours had been moved. He had been wronged, and he was simply upset about it.
Next steps: corrected Pankaj's hours and apologised to him. Booked a separate talk with Ritesh to ask what change he actually wants.

qa.q: What did Pankaj say had happened to his overtime hours?
qa.a: Pankaj said his overtime hours had been logged under someone else's name.

qa.q: Why did Sudha nearly tell Pankaj to come back later?
qa.a: Sudha was put off by the shouting and half assumed an upset person must be less reliable, which almost led to judging him wrongly.

qa.q: Which choice by Sudha turned the week around?
qa.a: Checking the logs before responding showed Pankaj had truly been wronged; correcting the hours and booking a separate talk with Ritesh treated each case on its facts.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt if Sudha had sent him away for being upset?
qa.a: He would have felt wronged twice, first by the moved hours and then by not being believed because he was angry.

grounding: A supervisor notices the difference between Ritesh's repeated stories of always being the sufferer and Pankaj's real, angry complaint, and checks the facts before judging.

Tuesday night
Simran cried in the office corridor today, and my first thought was: here we go again.
I know that's unkind. But in eight months of sitting next to her, every week has had a new villain. The printer technician was out to get her. The manager hates her. The canteen staff did it on purpose. I've started nodding without listening.
Today she said Harsh presented her budget sheet as his own in the client meeting. I nearly said "hmm" and walked on. Then I remembered watching her build that sheet, formula by formula, last Thursday.
So I said, "I saw you make it. Do you want me to tell the manager that?" She stopped crying and stared, like she didn't expect anyone to believe her.
Note to self: the pattern is real. So was this. Check before deciding.
Vijay

qa.q: What did Harsh present as his own?
qa.a: Harsh presented Simran's budget sheet as his own in the client meeting.

qa.q: Why was Vijay's first thought "here we go again"?
qa.a: Vijay felt tired of Simran's weekly stories with new villains and had stopped really listening, so the tears seemed like more of the same.

qa.q: What small step made Vijay's response fair?
qa.a: Vijay remembered watching Simran build the sheet and offered to tell the manager, checking the facts instead of judging by the old pattern.

qa.q: What might it have meant to Simran that Vijay believed her?
qa.a: She seemed surprised, as if she didn't expect to be believed, so it may have felt like relief at being taken seriously for once.

grounding: Vijay, who sits beside Simran and is tired of her weekly stories of villains, nearly dismisses a real grievance, then checks what was seen and backs her.

In the government school of the small town, the staffroom knew Imran's stories by heart. The headmaster was against him. The clerk lost his forms on purpose. The parents complained only about him. Ira, who taught maths across the table, had started tuning out.
Then, on Tuesday, Imran came in shouting. His leave for his sister's wedding had been cancelled at the last minute, while another teacher's leave on the same dates was approved. He slammed his bag down. "They always do this to me!"
Two colleagues rolled their eyes. Ira nearly did too.
But she went to the office and checked the leave register herself. Imran had applied first, with all the papers. The other application had come a week later.
Ira came back and said quietly, "Imran, you're right this time. It's in the register. Let's go to the headmaster together."
Imran stared at her, his anger turning into something like surprise.

qa.q: What was cancelled at the last minute?
qa.a: Imran's leave for his sister's wedding.

qa.q: How did Ira feel when Imran came in shouting?
qa.a: Ira felt tired and sceptical, nearly rolling her eyes, because she was used to his stories always casting others as villains.

qa.q: What did Ira do before judging Imran's complaint?
qa.a: She checked the leave register herself, found he had applied first, and offered to go with him to the headmaster.

qa.q: How did Imran react when Ira believed him?
qa.a: Imran felt surprised, his anger softening, perhaps because people usually dismissed him.

grounding: It shows a colleague distinguishing a habitual victim story from a real wrong by checking facts, remembering that real victims are not always calm.

In the Copenhagen design office, Ines had learned to sigh quietly whenever Emil started a sentence with "Of course, nobody told me." In Emil's stories, he was always overlooked, blamed and betrayed, and everyone else was careless or cruel.
On Friday, he burst into the kitchen, red in the face. "They presented my packaging design at the board meeting. With Karl's name on it. My design!"
Ines's first thought was, here we go. Her second thought was that she didn't actually know.
"Show me," she said.
Emil opened his laptop, hands shaking. There were the files, dated three weeks earlier, from his account. There was the email where he'd sent them to Karl. Karl's slide was the same design, without Emil's name.
Ines closed the laptop gently. "Emil, this is real. I'm sorry. Let's take the files to our manager, now."
Emil blinked, as if he hadn't expected anyone to believe him.

qa.q: Whose name was on the packaging design at the board meeting?
qa.a: Karl's name was on it.

qa.q: How did Ines feel when Emil burst in?
qa.a: Ines felt weary and doubtful, thinking "here we go," because Emil always cast himself as the one betrayed.

qa.q: What did Ines do that avoided unfair judgement?
qa.a: She asked to see the evidence, found the dated files and email, and offered to go with Emil to their manager.

qa.q: How did Emil feel when Ines believed him?
qa.a: Emil felt surprised and relieved, as if he hadn't expected anyone to believe him.

grounding: It shows a colleague setting aside her impression of a habitual victim to check facts, finding he was truly wronged despite his agitation.

passage: At the logistics firm's Thursday team meeting, Manoj again explained why the shipment delay wasn't his fault: the vendor had lied, IT had sabotaged him, and the manager "always had it in for him". Kiran had heard a version of this every month for a year; in each story Manoj was the one suffering and someone else was the villain. Then Tenzin spoke, voice sharp and shaking. Her client file had been deleted by someone else's login, and she had been blamed in an email to the whole team. She wasn't calm. She interrupted twice. A few colleagues rolled their eyes. "Another drama." Kiran almost did too, then remembered that Tenzin had never once complained in two years, and that a login record was something anyone could check. After the meeting Kiran walked over to Tenzin's desk. "Want help pulling the access log for the manager?" Tenzin's shoulders dropped. "Yes. Please."

qa.a: It had been deleted by someone else's login, and she had been blamed in an email to the whole team.

qa.q: What made Kiran hesitate before judging Tenzin?
qa.a: Kiran was tempted to dismiss her as dramatic, then felt doubtful of that reaction on remembering that Tenzin had never once complained in two years.

qa.q: How did Kiran avoid misjudging Tenzin?
qa.a: Kiran looked at her record and at facts anyone could check, like the access log, instead of her tone, and offered practical help.

qa.a: Tenzin likely felt unheard and more upset, since being truly wronged and then dismissed as drama adds a second hurt.
